rohitupadhyaay.caption:
News creators are keeping journalism alive in India!

Last week in London, I had the opportunity to speak at the Chevening South Asia Journalism Fellowship symposium on “Journalism in an Age of Big Tech and Authoritarianism,” alongside journalists and media leaders from the BBC, DW, the Reuters Institute, and journalists from across South Asia.

One idea stayed with me long after the discussion ended.

For many journalists across South Asia, social media was never just another distribution platform. It became a space where important stories could still be told when traditional institutions came under pressure from governments, advertisers, and corporate interests.

For years, many dismissed news creators as people chasing views, trends, and algorithms. But that perception is changing.

Today, independent news creators are investigating stories, holding power to account, reaching millions of people directly, and making journalism accessible to audiences that legacy media often fails to reach.

Of course, influence comes with responsibility. Credibility, accuracy, transparency, and accountability matter more than ever.

If creators can uphold these values, they will not just complement journalism. They will help strengthen democracy itself.

Here’s to a future where independent news creators continue to grow, ask difficult questions, and earn the public’s trust, one story at a time.

#Journalism #CreatorEconomy #NewsCreators #Chevening

Reality of Babool Charcoal! 
An invasive tree once introduced to stop the Thar Desert from spreading has now become a serious environmental and public health threat. Prosopis juliflora, commonly known as Vilayati Babul, is cut and burned to produce charcoal in traditional kilns. The toxic smoke directly affects workers, many from nomadic communities such as the Jogi, Nath and Kalbelia tribes. This video also highlights new findings on air pollution, depression, anxiety, vehicle emissions and lead pollution from ships. It also explores positive developments in clean energy and pollution control, featured in Chintan’s September 2026 edition of the free bilingual ON AIR Webzine.

Air pollution is hurting more than just our lungs. #airpollution #delhincr @chintan.india @nidhi_s_jamwal @ms.zerovedi #delhi #uttarakhand 

Most of us think air pollution only affects breathing. I thought so too. But after reading Chintan’s ON AIR magazine, I discovered that polluted air can also irritate our eyes and even damage the cornea. What surprised me even more was learning that this is not just a Delhi or Mumbai problem anymore. From the forests of Uttarakhand to villages in Rajasthan, from landfills in Mumbai to garbage-burning sites in Delhi, air pollution is affecting people across the country. In Uttarakhand, worsening forest fires are making the air so toxic that some children have been forced to cover their eyes with wet handkerchiefs for relief. Experts warn that pollutants released from these fires can travel deep into our lungs and even reach the brain through the bloodstream. Meanwhile, poor waste management, landfill emissions, factory dust, and open waste burning continue to expose millions to toxic air every day. Air pollution is no longer just an environmental issue. It is a public health emergency hiding in plain sight. This video is based on stories and research featured in Chintan’s bilingual monthly webzine ON AIR, which is available free to read. If this information surprised you as much as it surprised me, do share this video so more people understand what polluted air is really doing to our bodies.

Smart City by Devi Prasad Mishra #Poetry

Translation: 
We need a city like that.

A city with lots of bicycles,
and lots of trees to lean those bicycles against.

Trees with countless leaves,
fluttering like countless flags of dissent.

We need a city where, on a dusty road with little traffic,
there is a small triangular park in the corner,
a place where people can fall in love.

And no BJP president, whether at the national,
state, district, or neighbourhood level,
can book that park for a political gathering.

We need a city with a small hospital, even a modest one,
where the treatment for a father’s authoritarianism
is free,
and so is the treatment for a sister’s depression.

Let’s make their voices heard!🙏

When a treatment needs regulation, the answer cannot be to stop listening to the people affected by that decision.

Thousands of parents of children with autism are asking for something very basic: to be heard.

And the debate shouldn’t be reduced to “stem cells work” vs “stem cells don’t work.”

It should be about:
→ What evidence exists?
→ What research is still needed?
→ How do we protect families from unproven or unsafe treatments?
→ And what happens to children who were already undergoing treatment?

Because behind every clinical debate are real children, real parents and real lives.

They deserve to be heard! 

#autism #india

The police were checking hotel records and pulling out every reporter who'd come from Delhi- the cost we pay for showing reality.

In the heart of India, Madhya Pradesh. I pre-booked a hotel for 3 days with my team for a shoot.

But within a day, we were asked to vacate it. The reason given was a family function. We were a little doubtful, but still vacated it.

We took another hotel. Weirdly, wahan bhi, within a night, humein vacate karne ko bola gaya.

I was confused. But later we found out that the police are trying to hide the reality of the Balaghat district of Madhya Pradesh where more than 25 children had lost their lives to basic diseases like m*laria, m*asles, and malnutrition.

Log sadko pe aa kar insaaf maang rahe the. Lad rahe the for better healthcare facilities and more responsible systems.

I went there because it is important to show this side of India too.

But I was honestly scared. I was constantly being watched; the police had my Aadhaar details.

Lol, I wish such resources, such quick action, were used for the health and facilities of these villagers.

Turns out, the priority isn't fixing the reality. It's hiding it.

A district of Madhya Pradesh - Balaghat.
Rich in forests, biodiversity and minerals, yet many Adivasi communities living here continue to struggle with basic necessities.

Balaghat gives India manganese, copper and other minerals. But behind these resources is a reality that deserves attention: more than 25+ tribal children have lost their lives, while many others have faced illness, malnutrition and limited access to healthcare.

And Balaghat is not the only place where resource-rich communities face difficult realities.
Jharia gives India coal, while communities living here face the consequences of fires, land subsidence and displacement.

Jadugoda gives India uranium, while communities living around uranium mining have raised concerns about health and environmental impacts.

The resources may fuel our development, but the people living on these lands should not have to pay the price.

When I walked into Balaghat, I thought I was just covering a news report. But looking inside these mud homes, the silence of these everyday things completely broke my heart. Every object here tells the story of a real person and an unhealed pain.

Created by - @_stuti160_ & @ye_sham_mastaaani 

Kajal was only ten and dreamed of becoming a doctor. But when she got sick, no doctor came to help her. Sitting with her sister, watching her cry, hurt so deeply.

This water tank was built three years ago, but it just stands there, completely dry. On the ground, nothing changed. Families are still forced to drink, cook, and bathe in muddy red water every single day. 

When Roopal fell ill, no ambulance could come because there are no real roads. His father carried him on his back for miles through the mud just to find help. He spent every rupee he had, only to say:2 “Na baccha raha, na paisa.” 

This small diary tracks every sick person and pregnant mother in the village. These ASHA workers walk miles through the dirt every day to care for everyone. Yet they go months without getting paid a single rupee. 

I looked down at my phone in the middle of the village and saw 'No Service'. People talk about fast internet, but here, a mother cannot even make a quick phone call when her child is in danger. 

At the hospital, three sick kids were sharing one small, broken bed. Drips were tied with old strings and mothers were sitting on the floor. When help looks like this, poor families are forced into debt just to keep their children alive. 

Holding Kajal’s letter broke my heart. Just days before she died, she wrote: “Mujhe Bhartiya hone pe garv hai.” She loved her country so much, but lost her life to a fever that could have easily been cured.

“Ye sab ladkiya nahi karti” 
This is what she heard when she started driving a rickshaw.

I met Saiyyam aunty in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh.
Aur jaisa naam thik waisi hi vo..
3 saal se rickshaw chala rahi hai aur bas kabhi ruki nahi.. 
How surprising it is to see women doing something 
in a male dominated field 
and aise ek aurat ko apne liye ladna, 
stereotype todte hue dekhna.
Accha toh lagta hai 🥹

Society often tells women, 
“Ye kaam auraton ka nahi hai, tumse nahi ho paayga”
Lekin in sab baaton se ladd kar, apne liye khade rehna shows
ki auratein haar toh nahi maanne wali kabhi..

She was part of the ongoing protest. 
She helped protesters by transporting them for free.
Haste hue, dil se madad karte hue..

But what filled my heart the most was what she told me next. 
Women stop her on the road, look at her, and say,
"Aunty gaadi chala sakte hain, kuch bhi kar sakte hain. Toh hum kyun nahi?"

She never set out to inspire anyone. She was just living her life. 
But somewhere, another woman was watching, 
and for the first time, she felt "Hum bhi kar sakte hain."

Think about that. 
One woman's courage became another woman's permission.

Before I left, she held my hand a little longer and said,
"Ek baar milta hai jeevan... marne ki nahi sochna. 
Kuch bhi jeevan mein aaye hain toh karo."

She said it like it was nothing. But it felt like a blessing.

And then, with the warmest smile:
"Aapse milke, baat karke achha laga."

Aunty, mujhe bhi. Bohot, bohot zyada. 
I walked away lighter than I had come. 
Because some people don't give speeches or make a lot of noise. 
They just live so bravely that the people around them quietly begin to believe in themselves.

Aaj bhi kahin, koi ladki apni pehli himmat dhundh rahi hai. 
Shayad use bas ek aisi aurat chahiye, jo dikha de ki ho sakta hai.
Aur shayad, kisi ke liye, woh hum bhi ho sakte hain. ♥️

She is only 17. She is already a mother. And today, her child is fighting malaria.

I met a girl at a hospital in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh.
She had been married young because her family was extremely poor, and she never got the chance to study.

But her story is not an isolated one. Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, is facing a serious health crisis.

Children, mostly from marginalised Adivasi communities, are suffering from severe malnutrition and diseases like malaria and measles.

At one hospital, I met 10–15 parents whose children were suffering from malaria. For some of them, this was their first time seeing a hospital because they come from villages where basic healthcare facilities are almost non-existent. And the problems begin even before they reach the hospital.

In some villages, there is no mobile network. People have to travel almost 1 km just to make a phone call, even to call an ambulance.

There is a tap, but no water. There is a handpump, but the water that comes out is red.

We talk about Digital India. We talk about 5G.
But for some families, even making one simple phone call in an emergency is a struggle.

Inside the hospital, I saw a picture of India that was difficult to process: mothers sitting beside their sick children,
3–4 patients sharing the same bed, and new children arriving every day with malaria and measles.
